passage: I was in the courtyard of our block in Hyderabad when a visiting uncle bent to hug Rafiq, six, who stiffened and ducked away, arms crossed over his chest. The uncle laughed, "Come on, one hug!" Rafiq shook his head. "No hug." His mother Jahnavi stepped in. "He said no. Would a high-five do?" The uncle held up his palm and Rafiq slapped it, looking relieved. I couldn't tell if he was tired, shy or just didn't want to be touched, but his body was clear.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do when the uncle bent to hug him?
qa.a: He stiffened and ducked away, with his arms crossed over his chest.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's body suggest about how he felt, and what does the narrator say they couldn't tell?
qa.a: His stiffening and ducking suggest he was uncomfortable with the hug, and his relief at the high-five fits that. The narrator couldn't tell whether it was tiredness, shyness or not wanting to be touched.

qa.q: What can Jahnavi do to support Rafiq?
qa.a: She can keep respecting his signals and offer other ways to greet, such as a high-five, and encourage him to say no or tell a trusted adult if he is pressured.

qa.q: How might the uncle feel when Rafiq ducks away?
qa.a: He may feel a little rejected, but the high-five lets him greet Rafiq without making it about him.

grounding: A child pulls away from an unwanted hug, a valid signal that caring adults respect.

passage:
Day one: at the aunts' gathering in Dhaka, Zeenat, five, pulled back when a relative reached to pinch her cheek. Her mother Dilnaz said, "She'd rather wave." Zeenat waved.
Day three: at the park, a neighbour tried to lift Zeenat onto a swing. She stiffened, and Dilnaz said gently, "Zeenat, do you want help?" Zeenat shook her head and climbed herself.
Day six: Zeenat told her mother, "I don't like when they pinch. I can say no." Dilnaz hugged her, asking first.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do when the relative reached to pinch her cheek?
qa.a: She pulled back.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's stiffening on day three suggest about her feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uncomfortable about being lifted without asking. Her calm headshake and climbing by herself show she preferred to decide for herself.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz keep doing to help Zeenat with saying no?
qa.a: She can keep noticing her signals, speaking up for her when needed and praising her words, and tell her to speak to a trusted adult if pressure continues.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel on day six when her mother asks before hugging her?
qa.a: She may feel her body is her own and trust her mother more.

grounding: A child pulls back from touch she doesn't want, and adults respect it while she learns to say no.

passage: The wedding hall was packed, and Farida had five minutes to get Aadhya changed for the photos. On the way, a distant aunty grabbed Aadhya and squeezed her into a hug, kissing her cheek. Aadhya stiffened, ducked, and pushed at the aunty's arm. The aunty laughed and pulled her closer. Farida stepped in. “She doesn't want a hug right now. High five, Aadhya?” Aadhya gave a tiny high five. Walking away, Farida said, “You're allowed to say no. If anyone keeps doing it, tell me.”

qa.q: What did Farida offer instead of the hug?
qa.a: A high five.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's stiffening and ducking show about how she felt?
qa.a: They showed she was uncomfortable and did not want the hug. The aunty seemed to read it as shyness, but Aadhya was signalling no.

qa.q: How did Farida protect Aadhya, even in a rush?
qa.a: She stepped in straight away, spoke up for Aadhya, offered a high five instead, and told her she could say no and tell her if it happened again.

qa.q: How might the aunty see Farida's words?
qa.a: She might feel a little embarrassed or surprised, but she also learns that Aadhya's no should be respected.

grounding: A child stiffens and pulls away from an unwanted hug, and her mother respects the signal and teaches her she can say no and tell.

passage: At the colony gate, Anand Uncle from the next building bent down, ruffled Baljeet's hair and held out his arms. “Come, give Uncle a big hug!” Baljeet stepped back behind his mother, his body stiff. His mother said calmly, “He doesn't want to, and that's okay.” Anand Uncle straightened up and nodded. “Fair enough. High five, then?” Baljeet thought, then slapped his palm. At home, his mother said, “You can say, ‘No, thank you.’ And if someone doesn't stop, come and tell me.” Baljeet practised it on his teddy.

qa.q: What did Baljeet practise on his teddy?
qa.a: Saying, “No, thank you.”

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he stepped behind his mother?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable and did not want the hug, and his stiff body showed it. He may also have felt shy with Uncle.

qa.q: What did Baljeet's mother teach him at home?
qa.a: She gave him the words “No, thank you” and told him to come and tell her if someone doesn't stop.

qa.q: How did Anand Uncle respond, and what does it show?
qa.a: He accepted the no and offered a high five, which shows a caring adult respecting a child's signal.

grounding: A child pulls back from a neighbour's hug, the adults respect it, and he practises saying no and telling a trusted adult.

passage:
“Papa, can I not go to tuition tomorrow?”
Harish put down his phone. “What's happened, Ojas?”
“A big boy squeezes me in a hug. Really tight. I say stop and he doesn't.”
“How does it feel?”
“Scary. I can't breathe.”
Harish knelt beside him. “Thank you for telling me. It's not your fault, and you were right to say stop. Your body is yours.”
“Will you tell Miss?”
“Right now.” He called the tuition teacher while Ojas held his hand, and she promised to keep the boy away from Ojas and to speak to his parents that evening.

qa.q: What did Ojas say he does when the big boy hugs him?
qa.a: He says stop, and the boy doesn't stop.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling about the tight hugs?
qa.a: He felt scared and trapped, saying he couldn't breathe, and worried enough to want to skip tuition.

qa.q: What did Harish do that a caring adult should do?
qa.a: He listened, thanked Ojas, said it was not his fault and that he was right to say stop, and called the tuition teacher straight away while Ojas held his hand.

qa.q: How might the tuition teacher see Harish's call?
qa.a: The teacher would likely take it seriously and act, keeping the boy away from Ojas and speaking to his parents that evening.

grounding: A child's pulling away from tight hugs is a valid no; when the pressure continues he tells his father, who acts the same day.

passage:
Note from Tushar, school annual day, for Aditi's mother

After the dance, a visiting uncle of Aditi's came backstage and pulled her into a tight hug. Aditi went stiff, turned her face away and tried to wriggle out. He laughed and hugged her again.

I stepped in and said, "Aditi can wave or give a high-five instead." She waved. He shrugged and left.

Then I sat with Aditi. We practised saying, "No, thank you, I don't want a hug," and I told her she can always tell me or her mother if anyone keeps pushing. I am telling you today as well.

qa.q: What did the visiting uncle do after Aditi tried to wriggle out?
qa.a: He laughed and hugged her again.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she went stiff and turned her face away?
qa.a: She was most likely uncomfortable and upset about a hug she did not want, and her stiff body was a clear signal. She may also have been tired and overwhelmed after the dance.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that protected Aditi?
qa.a: Tushar stepped in with another choice, a wave or high-five, practised a clear "No, thank you" with her, reminded her she can tell a trusted adult, and informed her mother the same day.

qa.q: How might Aditi's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She would likely be glad Aditi's discomfort was noticed and respected, and able to follow up at home that evening.

grounding: It shows a child stiffening and pulling away from an unwanted hug, an adult respecting the signal, and the child practising saying no and telling.
